Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $p$ be the transition matrix of a countable state space $E$
([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]), so that
$p(x,y)\ge0$ and $\sum_{y\in E}p(x,y)=1$ for every $x\in E$. A **state measure**
is a function $\mu:E\to[0,+\infty)$ with $\mu(x)<+\infty$ for every $x$; it is
**nonzero** when $\mu(x)>0$ for at least one $x$. Such a measure $\mu$ is
**reversible** for $p$, and $\mu$ satisfies **detailed balance** for $p$, when

$$\mu(x)\,p(x,y)=\mu(y)\,p(y,x)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in E .$$

If in addition $\sum_{x\in E}\mu(x)=1$, then $\mu$ is a **reversible
probability distribution** for $p$.

Because each value $\mu(x)$ is finite and each transition entry lies in $[0,1]$,
every product $\mu(x)p(x,y)$ is a well-defined element of $[0,+\infty)$; the
identity is between nonnegative numbers and involves no subtraction of infinite
quantities. Every entry $p(x,x)$ satisfies the identity trivially, including
when $\mu(x)=0$. A state with $\mu(x)=0$ may have $p(x,\cdot)$ arbitrary; the
identity then forces $\mu(y)p(y,x)=0$ for all $y$, so no flow from the positive
support of $\mu$ enters $x$. The definition imposes no irreducibility,
aperiodicity or normalization hypothesis, and a nonzero reversible measure may
have infinite total mass; normalization to total mass one is stated separately.
The reversal interpretation of detailed balance is given by
[[thm-time-reversal-of-a-stationary-markov-chain]], and the lemma
[[lem-detailed-balance-implies-invariance]] shows that a reversible measure is
invariant even when its total mass is infinite.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Set $q_{xy}=\pi(x)P(x,y)$. By [F3], $q_{xy}=q_{yx}$; by [F1] its row sums are $\pi(x)$, and by [F2] its column sums are also $\pi(y)$. For a real-valued function $f$ define $\displaystyle \mathcal E(f)=\frac12\sum_{x,y}q_{xy}(f(x)-f(y))^2.$ Expanding the square and using these row and column sums gives $\mathcal E(f)=\langle f,(I-P)f\rangle_\pi$.

Suppose $f\ge0$ and its support has $\pi$-mass at most $1/2$. For $t\ge0$, let $S_t=\{x:f(x)^2>t\}$. The finite layer-cake identities give $\int_0^\infty\pi(S_t)\,dt=\sum_x\pi(x)f(x)^2$ and $\int_0^\infty Q(S_t,S_t^c)\,dt=\frac12\sum_{x,y}q_{xy}|f(x)^2-f(y)^2|$. Every nonempty $S_t$ is admissible in the definition of $\phi$, so the latter integral is at least $\phi\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2$. Apply [F5] to the finite weighted sum with weights $q_{xy}/2$ and the factors $f(x)-f(y)$ and $f(x)+f(y)$. It bounds the integral above by $\sqrt{\mathcal E(f)\cdot\frac12\sum_{x,y}q_{xy}(f(x)+f(y))^2}$; using $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ and the row and column sums makes the second factor at most $2\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2$. If $f\ne0$, division yields $\mathcal E(f)\ge(\phi^2/2)\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2$; for $f=0$ it is immediate.

Let $g$ be a real function with $\sum_x\pi(x)g(x)=0$. A weighted median $m$ exists by sorting the finitely many values of $g$ until their cumulative $\pi$-mass reaches $1/2$; hence each of $g_+=(g-m)_+$ and $g_-=(m-g)_+$ has support mass at most $1/2$. For every pair $x,y$, $((g-m)(x)-(g-m)(y))^2\ge(g_+(x)-g_+(y))^2+(g_-(x)-g_-(y))^2$. Therefore step 1.1 gives $\mathcal E(g)=\mathcal E(g-m)\ge\mathcal E(g_+)+\mathcal E(g_-)$.

Apply steps 2.1 and 2.2 to $g_+$ and $g_-$. Their squared norms sum to $\|g-m\|_{2,\pi}^2=\|g\|_{2,\pi}^2+m^2\ge\|g\|_{2,\pi}^2$ because $g$ has mean zero. Thus $\mathcal E(g)\ge(\phi^2/2)\|g\|_{2,\pi}^2$.

Detailed balance makes $P$ self-adjoint for $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\pi$, since exchanging $x,y$ in the finite sum proves $\langle f,Pg\rangle_\pi=\langle Pf,g\rangle_\pi$. Constants are $1$-eigenvectors. For any complex-valued $f$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz and the row sums give $|Pf(x)|^2=|\sum_yP(x,y)f(y)|^2\le\sum_yP(x,y)|f(y)|^2$. Summing against $\pi(x)$ and using stationarity gives $\|Pf\|_{2,\pi}\le\|f\|_{2,\pi}$. Thus every eigenvalue is at most $1$ and $1$ is the top eigenvalue. If a real function satisfies $Pf=f$, choose a state where it attains its maximum. Its value is a convex average of neighboring values, so every state reached with positive transition probability has the same maximum; irreducibility propagates this to every state. Thus the real $1$-eigenspace consists only of constants. For a complex $1$-eigenvector, its real and imaginary parts are real $1$-eigenvectors, so the same conclusion holds. By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis with first vector the normalized constant vector and eigenvalues $1=\lambda_1>\lambda_2\ge\cdots$. Expanding any mean-zero vector in the remaining basis vectors shows directly that its Rayleigh quotient for $I-P$ is a weighted average of $1-\lambda_j$, whose minimum is $1-\lambda_2$. Step 3.1 bounds every real mean-zero quotient below by $\phi^2/2$; applying that inequality to the real and imaginary parts gives the same bound for complex vectors. This proves the claim. A possible negative eigenvalue near $-1$ does not affect the algebraic gap.

derivations.claim: Write $H_J$ in blocks as $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^*&D\end{pmatrix}$ for $S\oplus S^\perp$. Then $\|B\|\le K$ and $D=Q_SH_1Q_S+JQ_SH_2Q_S\ge(J-K)I$ by [F1]–[F2]. For real $\lambda\le K$, $D-\lambda I\ge(J-2K)I>0$, so the Schur complement $\displaystyle S_\lambda=A-\lambda I-B(D-\lambda I)^{-1}B^*$ is defined and $0\le B(D-\lambda I)^{-1}B^*\le\epsilon_J I$.

The invertible block triangular change of variables completing the square in $\langle(H_J-\lambda)x,x\rangle$ gives the direct sum quadratic form of $S_\lambda$ and $D-\lambda I$. Since the latter is positive definite, the largest dimension of a subspace on which $H_J-\lambda I$ is negative definite equals the corresponding dimension for $S_\lambda$. This follows directly because the triangular change is an invertible linear map and hence preserves subspace dimension and signs of the quadratic form.

For $k=1,2$, the span of the first $k$ eigenvectors of $A$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $S$ on which the Rayleigh quotient of $H_J$ is at most $\mu_k$. If $H_J$ had fewer than $k$ eigenvalues at most $\mu_k$, that subspace would contain a nonzero vector orthogonal to its first $k-1$ eigenvectors, whose Rayleigh quotient would be strictly larger than $\mu_k$, a contradiction. Thus $\lambda_k(H_J)\le\mu_k\le K$.

Fix $k=1$ or $2$ and suppose $\lambda<\mu_k-\epsilon_J$. Then $\lambda<K$, and step 1.1 gives $S_\lambda\ge A-(\lambda+\epsilon_J)I$. Since $\lambda+\epsilon_J<\mu_k$, at most $k-1$ eigenvalues of $S_\lambda$ are negative. By step 2.1, at most $k-1$ eigenvalues of $H_J-\lambda I$ are negative. Letting $\lambda$ increase to $\mu_k-\epsilon_J$ proves $\lambda_k(H_J)\ge\mu_k-\epsilon_J$. The gap estimate follows by subtracting the bounds for $k=1,2$.

If $x=s+t$ is a unit eigenvector of eigenvalue $\lambda\le K$, its $S^\perp$ block equation is $B^*s+(D-\lambda I)t=0$. By step 1.1, $\|(D-\lambda I)^{-1}\|\le1/(J-2K)$; then [F2] yields $\|t\|\le K\|s\|/(J-2K)$. No lower bound on the compressed gap was used in this leakage estimate. For a counterexample to any gap conclusion from $J>2K$ alone, take $\dim S=2$, $H_1=0$, and $H_2=0$ on $S$ and $I$ on $S^\perp$; then $K=0$, every $J>0$ satisfies $J>2K$, and the lowest eigenvalue of $H_J$ has multiplicity two. Hence the separate compressed-gap condition is necessary.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a
non-negative operator $R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$,
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)$ is non-negative and

$$\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R))=\operatorname{tr}(R).$$

Here $\operatorname{End}(H)$ is the set of linear maps $H\to H$ as in
[[def-qc-partial-trace]], $I_H$ denotes the identity map $x\mapsto x$, and both
conclusions include zero-dimensional factors.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

For every linear map $A:H\to K$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces,

$$\|A\|_1=\operatorname{tr}_H\!\left(\sqrt{A^*A}\right).$$

Here $A^*A$ and its non-negative square root are endomorphisms of the domain
$H$; the trace is taken on $H$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner

derivations.claim: Fix $s_0\in[0,1]$. By [F1], the selected finite set of eigenvalues at $s_0$ is separated from its complement by the positive gap. Choose finitely many positively oriented closed contours whose interiors contain exactly this cluster and whose boundaries avoid the spectrum; for a sufficiently small neighborhood of $s_0$, the resolvent on these contours remains defined. Indeed, if $R_0(z)=(H(s_0)-zI)^{-1}$ and $\|H(s)-H(s_0)\|\|R_0(z)\|<1$ uniformly on the compact contour, then submultiplicativity [F3] makes the Neumann series for $I+(H(s)-H(s_0))R_0(z)$ convergent and gives the inverse.

On this neighborhood, [F2] and the scalar residue formula give the same Riesz projection as the definition: $\displaystyle P(s)=-\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\Gamma(H(s)-zI)^{-1}\,dz.$ To see this, diagonalize $H(s)$; the integral of $(\lambda-z)^{-1}$ is $-2\pi i$ when $\lambda$ is inside the contour and zero when it is outside, so the sum is exactly the projection onto the selected eigenspaces.

Put $R_z(s)=(H(s)-zI)^{-1}$. Differentiating $(H-zI)R_z=I$ gives $\dot R_z=-R_zH'R_z$ and differentiating again gives $\ddot R_z=2R_zH'R_zH'R_z-R_zH''R_z$. The contour is compact and stays uniformly in the resolvent set on this neighborhood, so these integrands and their first two derivatives are continuous uniformly in $z$. Differentiation under the finite contour integral is therefore valid, and step 2.1 makes $P$ twice continuously differentiable near $s_0$.

On the overlap of two such neighborhoods, each contour formula projects onto the same coherently followed eigenspaces by [F1]–[F2]; hence the local projections agree. Their first two derivatives consequently agree on overlaps, so the local $C^2$ representations patch to a global $C^2$ map on $[0,1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints.

derivations.claim: Fix $s$ and write $P=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda_P}P_\lambda$. The displayed definition makes $\widetilde X$ off-diagonal: $P\widetilde XP=Q\widetilde XQ=0$. On each band-to-complement block, $[H,\widetilde X]$ multiplies $-P_\lambda X\widehat R_\lambda$ by $\lambda-H|_Q$, giving $P_\lambda XQ$; on the reverse block it gives $-QXP_\lambda$. Summing yields $[H,\widetilde X]=PX-XP$.

Choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ of $\operatorname{ran}P$ adapted to the mutually orthogonal $P_\lambda$. For each basis vector $e_j$ in $\operatorname{ran}P_\lambda$, $Q\widetilde Xe_j=-\widehat R_\lambda QXe_j$, so [F6] gives $\sum_j\|Q\widetilde Xe_j\|^2\le g^{-2}\sum_j\|QXe_j\|^2\le m\|QXP\|^2/g^2$. For a unit vector $u=\sum_j u_je_j$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] yields $\|Q\widetilde XPu\|\le\sum_j|u_j|\|Q\widetilde Xe_j\|\le(\sum_j|u_j|^2)^{1/2}(\sum_j\|Q\widetilde Xe_j\|^2)^{1/2}$, proving $\|Q\widetilde XP\|\le\sqrt m\|QXP\|/g$. Since each $\widehat R_\lambda$ and $P_\lambda$ is self-adjoint, taking adjoints in the defining sum gives $\widetilde{X^*}=\widetilde X^*$. Applying the column estimate to $X^*$ and using [F5] gives $\|P\widetilde XQ\|\le\sqrt m\|PXQ\|/g$. Since $\widetilde X$ is off-diagonal, for $u=p+q$ one has $\|\widetilde Xu\|^2=\|P\widetilde XQq\|^2+\|Q\widetilde XPp\|^2$; hence its full norm is the maximum of the two block norms. This proves $\|\widetilde X\|\le\sqrt m\|X\|/g$.

On a local fixed Riesz contour put $R_z=(H-zI)^{-1}$ and $\widehat R_z=Q(H|_Q-zI)^{-1}Q$. Then $\widetilde X=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint R_zXR_z\,dz$. For $G(A,B)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint R_zAR_zBR_z\,dz$, using $[H-z,R_z]=0$ gives $\displaystyle [H,G(A,B)]=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint(AR_zBR_z-R_zAR_zB)\,dz=A\widetilde B-\widetilde A B.$ Indeed, $R_z[H-z,A]R_z=AR_z-R_zA$ and $R_z[H-z,B]R_z=BR_z-R_zB$; adding the two commutator contributions cancels the middle terms. Write $C=A\widetilde B-\widetilde A B$. On each band eigenspace $P_\lambda$, the Sylvester equations from this commutator give $\displaystyle PGQ=P\widetilde C Q,\qquad QGP=-Q\widetilde C P,$ because $P_\lambda\widetilde C Q=-P_\lambda C\widehat R_\lambda$ and $Q\widetilde C P_\lambda=-\widehat R_\lambda C P_\lambda$.

Differentiate $HP=PH$ and multiply on the left by $Q$ and on the right by each $P_\lambda$. The resulting Sylvester equation is $(H|_Q-\lambda I)Q\dot P P_\lambda=-Q\dot H P_\lambda$, so $Q\dot P P_\lambda=-\widehat R_\lambda\dot H P_\lambda$. Differentiating $P^2=P$ gives $P\dot P P=Q\dot P Q=0$; self-adjointness gives the other off-diagonal block by adjoint. These identities equal the reduced-resolvent formula for $\widetilde{\dot H}$, proving $\dot P=\widetilde{\dot H}$. Step 2.1 then gives $\|\dot P\|\le\sqrt m\|\dot H\|/g$.

The diagonal blocks follow by expanding $R_z=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda_P}P_\lambda/(\lambda-z)+\widehat R_z$. In $QGQ$, the only non-holomorphic terms have the middle resolvent in $P_\lambda$, and their integrals are $-\widehat R_\lambda A P_\lambda B\widehat R_\lambda$; terms with all three resolvents in $Q$ are holomorphic inside the contour. Hence $QGQ=-Q\widetilde A\widetilde BQ$. In $PGP$, terms with three band resolvents have zero integral because their rational integrands decay as $z^{-3}$ and all their poles lie inside the contour. The remaining terms have two band poles $\lambda,\mu$ and one $Q$ resolvent. Their scalar contour coefficient equals $\widehat R_\lambda^2$ if $\lambda=\mu$ by Cauchy's derivative formula, and equals $(\widehat R_\lambda-\widehat R_\mu)/(\lambda-\mu)=\widehat R_\lambda\widehat R_\mu$ if $\lambda\ne\mu$ by the resolvent identity. Thus $PGP=P\widetilde A\widetilde BP$. Together with step 2.2, these blocks prove $\displaystyle G(A,B)=(P-Q)(\widetilde A\widetilde B+\widetilde{A\widetilde B}-\widetilde{\widetilde A B}).$ All contours enclose the whole band; coincident band eigenvalues are grouped into one $P_\lambda$, and the complementary resolvent is holomorphic throughout the enclosed region.

Differentiating the contour formula and using $\dot R_z=-R_z\dot H R_z$ gives $\displaystyle \dot{\widetilde X}=\widetilde{\dot X}-G(\dot H,X)-G(X,\dot H).$ Apply step 3.2 to both $G$ terms and use $\dot P=\widetilde{\dot H}$ from step 3.1. $$\widetilde X=-\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda_P}\left(P_\lambda X\widehat R_\lambda+\widehat R_\lambda XP_\lambda\right),\qquad \widehat R_\lambda=Q(H|_{\operatorname{ran}Q}-\lambda I)^{-1}Q,$$
where $\Lambda_P$ is the set of distinct eigenvalues in $\operatorname{ran}P$ and $P_\lambda$ is the corresponding eigenspace projection. Then
$$\dot P=\widetilde{\dot H},\quad \|\widetilde X\|\le\frac{\sqrt m\|X\|}{g},\quad \|Q\widetilde X P\|\le\frac{\sqrt m\|QXP\|}{g},\quad \|P\widetilde X Q\|\le\frac{\sqrt m\|PXQ\|}{g},$$
$$\|\dot P\|\le\frac{\sqrt m\|\dot H\|}{g},\quad \|Q\ddot P P\|\le\frac{\sqrt m\|\ddot H\|}{g}+\frac{4m\|\dot H\|^2}{g^2},$$
and
$$\|Q\dot{\widetilde{\dot P}}P\|\le\frac{\sqrt m\|Q\ddot P P\|}{g}+\frac{2m\|\dot H\|\|\dot P\|}{g^2}.$$
The rank $m$ may count multiplicity; the argument only uses that the number of distinct band eigenvalues is at most $m$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

derivations.claim: Put $D(s)=[P'(s),P(s)]$. Since $P,P'$ are self-adjoint, $D^*=-D$, so $K_A(s)=TH(s)+iD(s)$ is self-adjoint. Let $U_A$ solve $iU_A'=K_AU_A$, $U_A(0)=I$; [F4] gives existence and uniqueness, and differentiating $U_A^*U_A$ gives unitarity. Differentiating $P^2=P$ yields $PP'P=0$ and $P'P+PP'=P'$, hence $[D,P]=P'$. Therefore $P$ solves $iP'=[K_A,P]$, and so does $F(s)=U_A(s)P(0)U_A(s)^*$. Both have initial value $P(0)$; uniqueness for this finite linear matrix ODE gives $F(s)=P(s)$, or equivalently $U_A(s)P(0)U_A(s)^*=P(s)$.

Define the unitary wave operator $\Omega(s)=U_A(s)^*U_T(s)$. Differentiating with the two evolution equations gives $\Omega'(s)=-U_A(s)^*D(s)U_T(s)$ and therefore $\Omega(s)=I-\int_0^sU_A(r)^*D(r)U_A(r)\Omega(r)\,dr$. The intertwining identity in step 1.1 implies that the conjugated kernel is off-diagonal relative to $P(0),Q(0)$ and that $\displaystyle Q(0)\Omega(s)P(0)=-\int_0^s Q(0)P'(r)[r]P(0)\Omega(r)P(0)\,dr,$ where $X[r]=U_A(r)^*X(r)U_A(r)$.

For any differentiable $X$, the commutator identity from [[lem-qa-36-jrs-finite-band-estimates]] and step 1.1 gives $\displaystyle \frac{d}{dr}\bigl(Q(0)\widetilde X[r]P(0)\bigr)=-iTQ(0)X[r]P(0)+Q(0)\dot{\widetilde X}[r]P(0).$ Indeed, $Q[H,\widetilde X]P=-QXP$, and the extra commutator with $iD/T$ has zero $QP$ block because $P[D,\widetilde X]Q=Q[D,\widetilde X]P=0$ when $D$ and $\widetilde X$ are off-diagonal. Integrating this identity by parts in step 2.1 with $X=P'$ and $Y(r)=P(0)\Omega(r)P(0)$ yields $\displaystyle Q(0)\Omega(s)P(0)=-\frac{i}{T}\left[Q(0)\widetilde{P'}[r]P(0)Y(r)\Big|_0^s-\int_0^sQ(0)\dot{\widetilde{P'}}[r]P(0)Y(r)\,dr-\int_0^sQ(0)\widetilde{P'}[r]P(0)P(0)\Omega'(r)P(0)\,dr\right].$ Here $\|Y(r)\|\le1$ and $P(0)\Omega'(r)P(0)=P(0)P'[r]Q(0)\Omega(r)P(0)$, because the $PQ$ block of $[P',P]$ is $-PP'Q$. The last integrand is therefore bounded by $\|Q\widetilde{P'}P\|\|P'\|\|Q(0)\Omega P(0)\|$. Repeating the same calculation with $P(0)$ and $Q(0)$ interchanged bounds $\|P(0)\Omega Q(0)\|$ by the same expression.

Use [F2] on the endpoint and derivative terms of step 3.1, and $\|Q\widetilde{P'}P\|\le\sqrt m\|P'\|/g$ on its product term. Since $\|Q(0)\Omega P(0)\|\le1$, this gives $\displaystyle \|Q(0)\Omega P(0)\|\le\frac1T\left[\frac{\sqrt m\|P'(0)\|}{g(0)}+\frac{\sqrt m\|P'(s)\|}{g(s)}+\int_0^s\left(\frac{\sqrt m\|QP''P\|}{g}+\frac{\sqrt m\|P'\|^2}{g}+\frac{2m\|H'\|\|P'\|}{g^2}\right)dr\right].$ Now $\|P'\|\le\sqrt m\|H'\|/g$. The first two integral terms are respectively at most $m\|H''\|/g^2+4m\sqrt m\|H'\|^2/g^3$ and $m\sqrt m\|H'\|^2/g^3$; the last is at most $2m\sqrt m\|H'\|^2/g^3$. Their sum gives exactly the integrand in $A_m(s)$, and the endpoint terms give its two endpoint summands. The same bound holds for $\|P(0)\Omega Q(0)\|$.

Unitary conjugation by $U_A$ and step 1.1 give $\displaystyle \|U_TP(0)U_T^*-P(s)\|=\|\Omega P(0)\Omega^*-P(0)\|=\|Q(0)\Omega P(0)-P(0)\Omega Q(0)\|.$ The last operator is off-diagonal with the two blocks bounded in step 4.1; its norm is the maximum of their norms, so it is at most $A_m(s)$. For a unit $\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P(0)$, $Q(s)U_T(s)\psi=U_A(s)Q(0)\Omega(s)P(0)\psi$ by step 1.1. Its squared norm is the transition probability and is at most $\|Q(0)\Omega(s)P(0)\|^2\le A_m(s)^2$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For finite-dimensional density operators $\rho,\sigma$,
$$0\le D(\rho,\sigma)\le1.$$
Moreover, $D(\rho,\sigma)=0$ iff $\rho=\sigma$, and $D(\rho,\sigma)=1$ iff their supports are orthogonal.

derivations.claim: Fix an assignment to all clock bits outside the local support of $h_\ell$. The subspace with that fixed spectator assignment and local clock state in $\{a_\ell,b_\ell\}$ is invariant; in the order $(a_\ell,b_\ell)$ the block is $\displaystyle \frac12\begin{pmatrix}I&-U_\ell^*\\-U_\ell&I\end{pmatrix}.$ The term is zero on every local pattern outside this pair. These mutually orthogonal blocks, together with the subspaces for those other local patterns, decompose the full register, so it suffices to inspect each displayed block and the zero action on the rest. For any data vectors $x,y$, its quadratic form is $\frac12\|y-U_\ell x\|^2\ge0$, and its kernel consists exactly of paired amplitudes $(x,U_\ell x)$. Hence $h_\ell$ is positive semidefinite on the full clock register.

On legal unary clocks, $a_\ell$ occurs only at $c_{\ell-1}$ and $b_\ell$ only at $c_\ell$. Define the unitary $W=\sum_{j=0}^NV_j\otimes|c_j\rangle\langle c_j|$ on that space. Since $V_\ell=U_\ell V_{\ell-1}$, conjugating the block from step 1.1 by $W$ makes every adjacent block $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}I&-I\\-I&I\end{pmatrix}$. Summing over edges gives $W^*H_{\rm prop}W=I_{\rm data}\otimes L_N/2$.

The quadratic form of $L_N$ is $\langle z,L_Nz\rangle=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|z_j-z_{j+1}|^2$, so its kernel is the constant clock vectors. Step 2.1 therefore gives exactly the displayed propagation kernel, with arbitrary data vector $\xi$.

On a legal clock, $H_{\rm input}$ vanishes except at $c_0$, where it is the data Hamming-weight operator $N_1=\sum_i|1\rangle\langle1|_i$. Since $V_0=I$, conjugation by $W$ leaves this block unchanged. For a kernel vector with data vector $\xi$, its input energy is $\langle\xi,N_1\xi\rangle/(N+1)$, which is zero exactly when $\xi$ lies in the one-dimensional span of $|0^n\rangle$. Thus $H_{\rm prop}+H_{\rm input}$ has the unique normalized kernel vector $|\eta\rangle$.

The clock penalty $H_{\rm clock}$ is positive semidefinite and has kernel exactly the legal unary strings: a binary string has no adjacent pattern $01$ exactly when all its $1$ bits precede all its $0$ bits. Each term of $H_{\rm final}$ is positive semidefinite by step 1.1 and the definitions of $H_{\rm input},H_{\rm clock}$. A zero-energy vector must therefore lie in the clock-penalty kernel and in the kernel identified in step 4.1. This proves uniqueness for the full final Hamiltonian.

Tracing the clock out of $|\eta\rangle\langle\eta|$ and using [F1] removes all cross terms between distinct $c_\ell$, giving $\displaystyle \rho_{\rm data}=\frac1{N+1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{N}|V_\ell0^n\rangle\langle V_\ell0^n|.$ For each $\ell\ge L$, the appended gates are identities, so $V_\ell|0^n\rangle=|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle:=U_L\cdots U_1|0^n\rangle$. There are $K+1$ such indices, and the other $L$ terms form a density operator $\sigma$ after normalization. Hence $\rho_{\rm data}=\frac{L}{N+1}\sigma+\frac{K+1}{N+1}|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle\langle\psi_{\rm out}|$.

By homogeneity of the trace norm in the definition of trace distance, the distance from $|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle\langle\psi_{\rm out}|$ is $\frac{L}{N+1}D(\sigma,|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle\langle\psi_{\rm out}|)\le L/(N+1)$ by [F3]. Since $K=\lceil2L/\varepsilon\rceil$ and $N=L+K$, we have $L/(N+1)\le L/K\le\varepsilon/2$.

derivations.claim: For the constructed path, the vectors $\eta_\ell$ are orthonormal because the prefixes $W_\ell$ are unitary and the clock states are orthonormal. The clock penalty vanishes on them. The input penalty annihilates $\eta_0$ because its data input is $|0^n\rangle$, and annihilates $\eta_\ell$ for $\ell>0$ because the first clock bit is $1$. Also $H_{\rm clock0}\eta_\ell=\ell\eta_\ell$. Each propagation term $h_\ell$ sends $\eta_{\ell-1}$ to $(\eta_{\ell-1}-\eta_\ell)/2$ and $\eta_\ell$ to $(\eta_\ell-\eta_{\ell-1})/2$, and annihilates the other history basis vectors, since $W_\ell=U_\ell W_{\ell-1}$. Thus $\mathcal S_0$ is invariant and the restricted matrix is $a\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,N)+tL_N$. For every $N\ge1$, the quadratic form of this abstract matrix at $x$ is $a\sum_{i=0}^N i|x_i|^2+t\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}|x_i-x_{i+1}|^2$, so both summands are positive semidefinite.

If $s=0$, then $H_0(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,N)$ and its unique normalized nonnegative ground vector is $e_0$. If $s=1$, then $H_0(1)=L_N/2$; its quadratic form is one half the sum of squared adjacent differences, so its kernel consists exactly of constant vectors, giving the stated uniform ground vector.

Suppose $0<s<1$, so $a,t>0$. The matrix is real symmetric with neighboring off-diagonal entries $-t$. By [F1], a complex eigenvector for the smallest eigenvalue exists; its real or imaginary part is a nonzero real eigenvector because the matrix and eigenvalue are real. Normalize that real eigenvector. Expanding any vector in the eigenbasis from [F1] shows its Rayleigh quotient is a weighted average of the eigenvalues, so this real eigenvector minimizes the quotient. Replacing its coordinates by their absolute values does not increase the Rayleigh quotient, since each edge contribution is $t(x_i-x_{i+1})^2$ and $(|x_i|-|x_{i+1}|)^2\le (x_i-x_{i+1})^2$; therefore a nonnegative ground vector $v$ exists. Its eigenvalue equation at any zero coordinate forces every adjacent coordinate to be zero, and connectedness of the path would then force $v=0$. Hence $v_i>0$ for every $i$.

The endpoint equation at vertex $0$ determines $v_1$ uniquely from $v_0$, and each interior equation determines $v_{i+1}$ from $v_i,v_{i-1}$. If $v_0=0$, the endpoint equation gives $v_1=0$ and recurrence gives $v=0$, impossible. Thus every eigenvector at a fixed eigenvalue is determined by its first coordinate, so the ground eigenspace is one-dimensional.

Write $E$ for the ground eigenvalue and $d_i=v_i-v_{i+1}$ for $0\le i<N$. The endpoint and interior eigenvalue equations give $\displaystyle d_0=\frac{E}{t}v_0,\qquad d_i-d_{i-1}=\frac{E-ai}{t}v_i\quad(1\le i<N),\qquad d_{N-1}=\frac{aN-E}{t}v_N.$ The ground energy satisfies $E\ge0$ because both terms in $H_0(s)$ are positive semidefinite. Testing the normalized constant vector gives $E\le aN/2$, because its Laplacian energy is zero and the average of $0,1,\ldots,N$ is $N/2$. Therefore $d_0\ge0$ and $d_{N-1}\ge0$.

Since $a>0$ and each $v_i>0$, the increments $d_i-d_{i-1}$ in step 3.2 are nonnegative while $ai\le E$ and nonpositive after $ai\ge E$. Thus the sequence $(d_i)$ first does not decrease and then does not increase; every one of its entries is at least the smaller of its two endpoint entries. Step 3.2 makes both endpoints nonnegative, so every $d_i\ge0$. This proves $v_i\ge v_{i+1}$ and completes the remaining case.

Let $N\ge1$, $s\in[0,1]$, $a=1-s$, $t=s/2$, and let $L_N$ be the graph Laplacian of the path with vertices $0,1,\ldots,N$. Define the clock matrix
$$H_0(s)=a\,\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,N)+tL_N.$$
For each $s\in[0,1]$, its smallest eigenvalue is simple and has a normalized nonnegative eigenvector $v(s)=(v_0,\ldots,v_N)$ satisfying
$$v_0\ge v_1\ge\cdots\ge v_N\ge0.$$
For $s>0$ the vector is strictly positive; at $s=0$ it is $e_0$ and its tail coordinates are zero. At $s=1$ it is the uniform vector.

For a path produced by [[alg-qa-36-five-local-history-path]], set $W_0=I$, $W_\ell=U_\ell\cdots U_1$ and $\eta_\ell=W_\ell|0^n\rangle\otimes|c_\ell\rangle$. The all-zero-input history sector $\mathcal S_0=\operatorname{span}\{\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_N\}$ is invariant under $H(s)$, and its restriction has matrix $H_0(s)$ in this orthonormal history basis.

Let $\Omega$ be a finite set with $|\Omega|\ge2$. Let $P=(P(x,y))_{x,y\in\Omega}$ be an irreducible row-stochastic matrix and let $\pi$ be a strictly positive stationary probability satisfying detailed balance
$$\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(y)P(y,x).$$
For $S\subseteq\Omega$, put $Q(S,S^c)=\sum_{x\in S,\,y\notin S}\pi(x)P(x,y)$, and define the conductance
$$\phi=\min_{0<\pi(S)\le1/2}\frac{Q(S,S^c)}{\pi(S)}.$$
If $1=\lambda_1>\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ are the eigenvalues of $P$ in the weighted inner product $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi=\sum_x\pi(x)f(x)\overline{g(x)}$, then the algebraic gap satisfies
$$1-\lambda_2\ge\frac{\phi^2}{2}.$$
No absolute-gap or aperiodicity assertion is made.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

derivations.claim: On legal clock $c_i$, $H_{\rm clock0}$ has eigenvalue $i$; the propagation terms have diagonal entries $1/2$ at the endpoints, $1$ internally, and adjacent entries $-1/2$. Therefore the clock matrix is the displayed $H_0(s)=aD+tL_N$, where $a=1-s$, $t=s/2$, and $D=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,N)$.

If $0\le s\le1/6$, the Rayleigh quotient at $e_0$ gives the ground eigenvalue $E_0\le t$. On the codimension-one subspace $e_0^\perp$, $D\ge I$ and $L_N\ge0$, so every Rayleigh quotient there is at least $a$. If the second eigenvalue $E_1$ were below $a$, the span of eigenvectors for the two lowest eigenvalues would have dimension at least two and would contain a nonzero vector orthogonal to $e_0$; its quotient, as an eigenbasis expansion supported on eigenvalues at most $E_1$, would be at most $E_1<a$, a contradiction. Hence $E_1\ge a$, and $E_1-E_0\ge a-t=1-3s/2\ge3/4$.

Now suppose $s\ge1/6$, so $t\ge1/12$, and let $v$ be the normalized positive ground vector from [F1], with eigenvalue $E_0$. Set $\pi_i=v_i^2$, so $\sum_i\pi_i=1$ and $\pi_0\ge\pi_1\ge\cdots\ge\pi_N>0$. For a vector $f=(f_i)$ with $\sum_i\pi_i f_i=0$, set $x_i=v_if_i$; then $x\perp v$ and $\|x\|^2=\sum_i\pi_i|f_i|^2$. The eigenvalue equation $H_0v=E_0v$, expanded edge by edge, gives the ground-state identity $\displaystyle \langle x,(H_0-E_0I)x\rangle=t\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}v_iv_{i+1}|f_i-f_{i+1}|^2.$ Indeed, the diagonal coefficient at vertex $i$ after subtracting $E_0$ is $t$ times the sum of neighboring ratios $v_j/v_i$; multiplying by $v_i^2|f_i|^2$ assigns $t v_iv_j|f_i|^2$ to each incident edge, and the off-diagonal term supplies $-2t v_iv_j\operatorname{Re}(\overline f_i f_j)$.

Since $v_i\ge v_{i+1}$, each edge weight satisfies $v_iv_{i+1}\ge\pi_{i+1}$. Define a continuous-time reversible path chain with stationary masses $\pi_i$ and symmetric edge conductances $c_i=\pi_{i+1}$: its rate from $i$ to $i+1$ is $c_i/\pi_i=\pi_{i+1}/\pi_i\le1$, and its reverse rate is $c_i/\pi_{i+1}=1$. Each total exit rate is at most $2$. Let $Q$ be its generator and $P=I+Q/2$. Then $P$ is row-stochastic, reversible with stationary law $\pi$, and irreducible, and its Dirichlet form is $\langle f,(I-P)f\rangle_\pi=\frac12\sum_i c_i|f_i-f_{i+1}|^2$.

For any set $S$ with $0<\pi(S)\le1/2$, if $0\in S$, choose the largest $k$ for which $\{0,\ldots,k\}\subseteq S$. Then $k<N$, edge $(k,k+1)$ crosses the cut, and the tail mass is at least $1/2$. Monotonicity gives $\sum_{j=k+1}^N\pi_j\le N\pi_{k+1}$, so $\pi_{k+1}\ge1/(2N)$. The chain flow across the edge is $c_k/2=\pi_{k+1}/2$, hence $Q_P(S,S^c)/\pi(S)\ge1/(2N)$. If $0\notin S$, put $k=\min S-1$; then $S\subseteq\{k+1,\ldots,N\}$ and $\pi(S)\le N\pi_{k+1}$, while the crossing flow is again $\pi_{k+1}/2$, giving the same ratio bound. Thus $\phi(P)\ge1/(2N)$.

By [F2], $1-\lambda_2(P)\ge1/(8N^2)$. The generator gap is twice this number because $P=I+Q/2$, so its Dirichlet-form Poincaré constant is at least $1/(4N^2)$. For any $x\perp v$, set $f_i=x_i/v_i$; then $\sum_i\pi_i f_i=0$. The ground-state identity in step 2.2 and $v_iv_{i+1}\ge c_i$ give $\langle x,(H_0-E_0I)x\rangle\ge t/(4N^2)\|x\|^2$. By [F3], expand $x$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis of $H_0$ with $v$ as its simple ground vector; choose $x$ to be a unit eigenvector for $E_1$, orthogonal to $v$. Its quotient is exactly $E_1-E_0$, so the established lower bound applies to this $x$. Thus $E_1-E_0\ge t/(4N^2)\ge1/(48N^2)$ for $s\ge1/6$. Together with step 2.1, this proves the uniform bound.

Let $V$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with inner product linear in its first argument. A **finite adiabatic path** is a family $H(s):V\to V$ of linear endomorphisms ([[def-linear-map]]) indexed by $s\in[0,1]$, whose matrix entries are twice continuously differentiable in $s$ and such that $H(s)=H(s)^*$ for every $s\in[0,1]$. A **coherently followed spectral band** is a norm-continuous family of orthogonal projections $P(s):V\to V$ indexed by $s\in[0,1]$, of one fixed rank $m\ge1$, commuting with $H(s)$, whose range is a sum of full eigenspaces and which locally continues the same isolated cluster. For a finite union of positively oriented circles $\Gamma$, define $\oint_\Gamma F(z)\,dz$ as the sum of the parameterized integrals $\int_0^{2\pi}F(c+re^{it})ire^{it}\,dt$ over its circle components. Local continuation means that on each neighborhood there is such a contour enclosing exactly the selected cluster and
$$P(s)=-\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\Gamma(H(s)-zI)^{-1}\,dz.$$
With $Q(s)=I-P(s)$, define the **full gap**
$$g(s)=\min\{|\lambda-\mu|:\lambda\in\sigma(H(s)|_{\operatorname{ran}P(s)}),\ \mu\in\sigma(H(s)|_{\operatorname{ran}Q(s)})\}.$$
If $Q(s)=0$, the full gap is $+\infty$. Admissible gapped paths have a uniform full gap $\inf_{s\in[0,1]}g(s)>0$. Distinct eigenvalues inside the band may cross; its total rank remains $m$.

For a real parameter $T\in\mathbb R$, the slow-time propagator $U_T$ is the unique solution of
$$i\frac{d}{ds}U_T(s)=T H(s)U_T(s),\qquad U_T(0)=I.$$
Identifying complex coordinates with real and imaginary parts reduces this to a real finite matrix ODE ([[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]); differentiating $U_T(s)^*U_T(s)$ shows it stays unitary.

An instance also supplies an explicit preparation isometry $A_0:\mathbb C^m\to V$ with image $\operatorname{ran}P(0)$ and its declared preparation cost. For a rank-one band this means a specified unit vector $\psi_0\in\operatorname{ran}P(0)$ and a circuit preparing it; for a rank-$m$ band it is an orthonormal frame, not just the matrix $H(0)$ or the projector $P(0)$. Given an input density operator $\rho_{\rm in}$ on $\mathbb C^m$, the evolved output is $\rho_T=U_T(1)A_0\rho_{\rm in}A_0^*U_T(1)^*$. This is a density operator: for $W=U_T(1)A_0$, $W^*W=A_0^*U_T(1)^*U_T(1)A_0=I$ by isometry and unitarity; hence $W\rho_{\rm in}W^*$ is nonnegative by its quadratic form, and $\operatorname{tr}(W\rho_{\rm in}W^*)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{\rm in}W^*W)=1$ by trace cyclicity ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]], [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]], [[thm-trace-of-ab-equals-trace-of-ba]]). A rank-one input is the pure-state projector ([[def-qc-pure-state-and-ray]], [[def-qc-density-operator]]). A supplied target density operator $\sigma$ on $V$ is compared with $\rho_T$ by trace distance $D(\rho_T,\sigma)$ ([[def-qc-trace-distance]]). A finite output POVM on $V$ and an accepting outcome set may be supplied; its success probability is the sum of the corresponding POVM probabilities ([[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]], [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]). A finite projective measurement on $V$ may also be supplied, with success probability given by its projective outcome law ([[def-qc-projective-measurement]], [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]]); this is a special case of the POVM interface. The model is mathematical and includes no physical postulate.

An **adiabatic path access instance** consists of a finite path model ([[def-qa-36-finite-adiabatic-path-model]]), its exact initial preparation circuit $A_0$ and cost $C_{\rm init}$, a finite term count $r$, and a uniform description
$$H(s)=\sum_{j=1}^r c_j(s)H_j,$$
where the $H_j$ are stated finite-dimensional self-adjoint operators and the real coefficient functions $c_j$ have explicit rational binary inputs, uniform evaluation procedures, certified value errors and certified first-derivative bound $M_1\ge\sup_s\|H'(s)\|$. The access declaration provides, for every allowed time code $u$, either the exact term operation $e^{-iuH_j}$ as a named oracle with its query charge, or a full-list uniform circuit family $V_j(u)$ with a certified bound $\|V_j(u)-e^{-iuH_j}\|\le\eta_j(u)$. Each inverse or controlled call is available only when separately declared. This is the finite term-list access interface of [[def-qa-20-simulation-error-and-cost-model]] and [[def-qa-20-term-list-access-model]].

The resource record lists separately: $C_{\rm init}$; the term count $r$; all term-oracle queries; controlled and inverse calls; gate, clean-ancilla and dirty-ancilla counts; coefficient-precision bits; full circuit-description bits; uniform generator time; and the continuous evolution time $T$. If a physical energy-normalized action is used, it also records $T\sup_s\|H(s)\|$. A missing coordinate is unavailable, not zero. No arbitrary matrix description or spectral projector supplies an initial preparation, term exponential, controlled call, inverse, coefficient evaluator, or circuit generator for free.

**Input:** An adiabatic path access instance from [[def-qa-36-adiabatic-resource-model]], a nonnegative finite exact time code $T$ from [[def-qa-20-term-list-access-model]], a rational tolerance $0<\varepsilon\le1$, and finite rational certificates $M_1\ge\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|H'(s)\|$ and $B\ge0$. The coefficient functions are real and have the uniform evaluation procedures and error certificates in the access instance. Each requested coefficient approximation is a finitely encoded real rational. The certificate $B$ bounds, for every sampled grid point and its supplied approximations, the commutator sum of the frozen self-adjoint summands. The access record provides supported term-time calls for every product-formula call below, with the requested certified operator errors. If any required coefficient, call, or certificate is unavailable, the algorithm returns no circuit.

**Output:** A finite access schedule that composes the supplied preparation, the segment calls and the declared output procedure, with the requested error budget and separately recorded supplied and generated resources. Each term call uses its declared provider: a supplied circuit-family call or a named-oracle call with its query charge. If all required operations are circuit families, the schedule expands into their composed circuit; otherwise it records each call using its declared provider, including every named-oracle query.

2. If $T>0$, set
$$q=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{3TM_1}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\right\},\qquad \tau=T/q.$$
These are computable finite integers and a supported time code. For each $j=0,\ldots,q-1$, let $s_j=j/q$ and request rational coefficient approximations $\widetilde c_{jk}$ defining $\widetilde H_j=\sum_{k=1}^{M}\widetilde c_{jk}H_k$ with certificate $\|\widetilde H_j-H(s_j)\|\le\varepsilon/(3T)$.

$$r_{\rm PF}=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{3q\tau^2B}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\right\}.$$
For each $j=0,\ldots,q-1$ in increasing order, and each product-formula substep $a=1,\ldots,r_{\rm PF}$, execute term calls for $k=M,M-1,\ldots,1$ at time code $(\tau/r_{\rm PF})\widetilde c_{jk}$. Each of the $qMr_{\rm PF}$ calls is supplied with operator error at most $\varepsilon/(6qMr_{\rm PF})$.

4. Execute the $q$ segment call sequences in increasing $j$ after $A_0$, then perform the declared output procedure. Record initial preparation, term queries, gates, ancillary wires, coefficient bits, circuit-description bits, generator time and $T$ separately. If any required coefficient evaluation, time code or term-exponential access is unavailable, this algorithm has no output schedule under the declared model.

Operator products are written in their ordinary left-to-right algebraic order, so the rightmost factor acts first on a vector. For an integer $r\ge1$, the $r$-step first-order approximation at time $t$ is $S_1(t/r)^r$. Each exponential is the finite-matrix evolution of [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]]; this definition does not identify the product with $e^{-itH}$ when terms fail to commute.

finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

A supported time code is a finite expression whose leaves are rational numbers or symbols $\rho_q$ denoting the unique positive real root of $x^q=4$ for an odd integer $q\ge1$; [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] gives a unique nonnegative root; it is positive because $0^q=0\ne4$. The operator-norm error is measured on the induced target operation. The provider specifies how each supported code is passed to the generator and records its actual description length and generation time; no polynomial bound is inferred. This is an explicit access promise, not a claim that every matrix has such a family.

For each supported call the input records its named-oracle query counts, gate count, ancillary wires, description bits, coefficient bits, and classical generation cost. Let $N\ge1$ be the number of propagation steps. On the legal-clock block with the zero data input, remove the input penalty and conjugate by the prefix unitaries as in [[lem-qa-36-history-state-ground-and-output]]. The resulting clock matrix is
$$H_0(s)=(1-s)\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,N)+\frac{s}{2}L_N,$$
where $L_N$ is the path Laplacian. Its ground eigenvalue is simple and its spectral gap is at least $1/(48N^2)$ for every $s\in[0,1]$. In particular, the restricted clock gap is $\Omega(N^{-2})$ uniformly along the path.

Let $N\ge1$, $s\in[0,1]$, $a=1-s$, $t=s/2$, and let $L_N$ be the graph Laplacian of the path with vertices $0,1,\ldots,N$. Define the clock matrix
$$H_0(s)=a\,\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,N)+tL_N.$$
For each $s\in[0,1]$, its smallest eigenvalue is simple and has a normalized nonnegative eigenvector $v(s)=(v_0,\ldots,v_N)$ satisfying
$$v_0\ge v_1\ge\cdots\ge v_N\ge0.$$
For $s>0$ the vector is strictly positive; at $s=0$ it is $e_0$ and its tail coordinates are zero. At $s=1$ it is the uniform vector.

For a path produced by [[alg-qa-36-five-local-history-path]], set $W_0=I$, $W_\ell=U_\ell\cdots U_1$ and $\eta_\ell=W_\ell|0^n\rangle\otimes|c_\ell\rangle$. The all-zero-input history sector $\mathcal S_0=\operatorname{span}\{\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_N\}$ is invariant under $H(s)$, and its restriction has matrix $H_0(s)$ in this orthonormal history basis.

Let the five-local path in [[alg-qa-36-five-local-history-path]] have $N=L+K$ gates, including its $K$ identity gates, and let $V_0=I$ and $V_\ell=U_\ell\cdots U_1$. On the legal unary-clock space, the propagation Hamiltonian has kernel
$$\left\{\frac1{\sqrt{N+1}}\sum_{\ell=0}^{N}V_\ell\xi\otimes|c_\ell\rangle:\xi\in(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\right\}.$$
After adding $H_{\rm input}$, this kernel is one-dimensional and its unit vector is
$$|\eta\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt{N+1}}\sum_{\ell=0}^{N}V_\ell|0^n\rangle\otimes|c_\ell\rangle.$$
The full $H_{\rm final}$ also has this unique ground state. Its data-register marginal is at trace distance at most $L/(N+1)\le\varepsilon/2$ from the specified circuit output state.

Let $\mathcal H=S\oplus S^\perp$ be finite-dimensional, let $H_1=H_1^*$ with $\|H_1\|\le K$, and let $H_2=H_2^*\ge0$ satisfy $H_2|_S=0$ and $H_2|_{S^\perp}\ge I$. For $J>2K$, set $H_J=H_1+JH_2$, and let $\mu_1\le\mu_2\le\cdots$ be the eigenvalues of the compression $A=P_SH_1|_S$, where $\dim S\ge2$. With $\epsilon_J=K^2/(J-2K)$, the two smallest eigenvalues of $H_J$ obey
$$\mu_k-\epsilon_J\le\lambda_k(H_J)\le\mu_k\quad(k=1,2).$$
Consequently $\lambda_2(H_J)-\lambda_1(H_J)\ge(\mu_2-\mu_1)-\epsilon_J$; positivity of this bound requires the separate condition $\epsilon_J<\mu_2-\mu_1$. Every unit eigenvector $x=s+t$ of $H_J$ with eigenvalue $\lambda\le K$ also satisfies $\|t\|\le K\|s\|/(J-2K)$. Thus $J>2K$ alone supplies no general gap conclusion.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal S$ be the subspace of legal unary clocks. The prefix conjugation from [[lem-qa-36-history-state-ground-and-output]] preserves each clock basis state and makes $H_{\rm prop}$ equal to $L_N/2$ on the clock. Since the input penalty acts only at $c_0$ and the prefix at $c_0$ is the identity, the compression of $H_1(s):=H(s)-JH_{\rm clock}$ to $\mathcal S$ decomposes, in the computational basis $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, as $\displaystyle H_x(s)=H_0(s)+|x|\,|c_0\rangle\langle c_0|,$ where $H_0(s)$ is the zero-input clock block and $|x|$ is Hamming weight.

The $x=0$ block has simple ground energy $E_0$ and gap $\Delta\ge1/(48N^2)$ by [F1]–[F2]. Write $p=|v_0|^2$. Since $0\le v_i\le v_0$ and $\sum_i|v_i|^2=1$, $p\ge1/(N+1)>0$. Also $\Delta\le2$: the compression of $H_0(s)$ to $S=\operatorname{span}\{e_0,e_1\}$ is positive and has trace at most $2$ (for $N=1$ its trace is $a+2t=1$, and for $N\ge2$ it is $a+3t=1+s/2\le3/2$). If $u_0$ is a normalized ground vector, the two-dimensional space $S$ contains a nonzero vector $z\perp u_0$. Its Rayleigh quotient is at least $E_1$ by expansion in an orthonormal eigenbasis, while the quotient is at most the largest eigenvalue of the compression to $S$, hence at most its trace $2$. Thus $E_1\le2$ and, since $E_0\ge0$, $\Delta=E_1-E_0\le2$.

For any $x\ne0$, put $r=|x|\ge1$ and $R=|c_0\rangle\langle c_0|$. The spectral gap of the zero-input block gives $H_0-E_0I\ge\Delta(I-|v\rangle\langle v|)$, and $rR\ge R$. Thus $\displaystyle H_x-E_0I\ge B:=\Delta(I-|v\rangle\langle v|)+R.$ If $p<1$, set $w=(c_0-\sqrt p\,v)/\sqrt{1-p}$. On the two-dimensional span of $v$ and $c_0$, the matrix of $B$ in the orthonormal basis $v,w$ has trace $1+\Delta$ and determinant $p\Delta$. Its smaller eigenvalue is at least its determinant divided by its trace, hence at least $p\Delta/(1+\Delta)$. On the orthogonal complement, $B=\Delta I$, so this bound applies to the whole space. If $p=1$, then $c_0=v$ and $B$ has eigenvalues $1$ on $v$ and $\Delta$ on $v^\perp$, so $B\ge\min\{1,\Delta\}I\ge\Delta/(1+\Delta)I$. Thus in either case $B\ge p\Delta/(1+\Delta)I$. By $\Delta\le2$, every nonzero-input block has ground energy at least $E_0+\Delta p/3\ge E_0+1/[144N^2(N+1)]$.

The legal compression therefore has unique ground in the $x=0$ block and gap at least $\displaystyle \min\left\{\frac1{48N^2},\frac1{144N^2(N+1)}\right\}=\frac1{144N^2(N+1)}\ge\Delta_0.$ The last inequality is equivalent to $3(N+1)^2\ge2N^2$, which holds for every $N\ge1$.

On the full register, $H_2=H_{\rm clock}$ is positive, vanishes exactly on $\mathcal S$, and is at least $I$ on $\mathcal S^\perp$: every illegal binary clock string contains at least one adjacent $01$ pair. To bound $H_{\rm prop}$, fix an assignment of all clock bits outside the local support of a term $h_\ell$. On the two local pattern states $a_\ell,b_\ell$, the block is $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}I&-U_\ell^*\\-U_\ell&I\end{pmatrix}$; it has eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ because $U_\ell$ is unitary, and $h_\ell$ is zero on the other local patterns. Thus $0\le h_\ell\le I$, $\|h_\ell\|\le1$, and $0\le H_{\rm prop}\le NI$. Also $\|H_{\rm input}\|\le n$ and $\|H_{\rm clock0}\|\le N$, by their sums of $n$ and $N$ projections. Hence $H_1(s)=H_{\rm input}+(1-s)H_{\rm clock0}+sH_{\rm prop}$ is self-adjoint and $\|H_1(s)\|\le n+(1-s)N+sN=n+N\le K_0$. The legal dimension is $2^n(N+1)\ge2$, so [F4] applies to its first two eigenvalues with $K=K_0$.

For this $J$, $J>2K_0$ and $\displaystyle \epsilon_J=\frac{K_0^2}{J-2K_0}<\frac{\Delta_0}{4}.$ The perturbation bounds in [F4] give $\lambda_1(H(s))\le\mu_1$ and $\lambda_2(H(s))\ge\mu_2-\epsilon_J$, where $\mu_2-\mu_1\ge\Delta_0$ by step 4.1. Thus the full gap is at least $\Delta_0-\epsilon_J>3\Delta_0/4$ for every $s$. Its positivity makes the ground state unique, and $\Delta_0=\Theta(N^{-3})$ gives the stated asymptotic gap.

**Input:** A full-list uniform circuit on $n\ge1$ qubits with $L\ge1$ listed gates $U_1,\ldots,U_L$, each acting on at most two data qubits, and a rational tolerance $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Circuit products act right to left ([[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]). The computation is applied to the explicitly supplied all-zero input preparation $A_0$; its wire and preparation cost $C_{\rm init}$ is recorded by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]] and [[def-qa-36-adiabatic-resource-model]]. The path-access input also supplies uniform term-time providers for the constructed term list, exact coefficient evaluation, supported time codes and certified call errors required by [[alg-qa-36-discretized-path-simulation]].

**Output:** The explicit finite term list and linearly interpolated Hamiltonian path $H(s)$, together with the supplied initial preparation and resource coordinates, plus the evolution access schedule and data-register output produced by steps 5–7 when the required access providers are available. The schedule uses the declared circuit-family or named-oracle provider for each term call and records its corresponding resource charge.

1. Set $K=\lceil2L/\varepsilon\rceil$ and $N=L+K$. Append $K$ identity gates, writing $U_\ell=I$ for $L<\ell\le N$. Use data space $(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}$ and an ordered $N$-qubit clock register ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]). Its legal unary clock basis is
$$|c_\ell\rangle=|1^\ell0^{N-\ell}\rangle,\qquad0\le\ell\le N.$$

2. Let $H_{\rm clock}=\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}|01\rangle\langle01|_{{\rm clock}_j,{\rm clock}_{j+1}}$ and
$$H_{\rm input}=\sum_{i=1}^n |1\rangle\langle1|_{{\rm data}_i}\otimes|0\rangle\langle0|_{{\rm clock}_1},\qquad H_{\rm clock0}=\sum_{j=1}^N|1\rangle\langle1|_{{\rm clock}_j}.$$
The first tensor factor is the data register. The zero-summand convention applies when an index range is empty.

3. For each transition $\ell-1\to\ell$, specify two local clock patterns $a_\ell,b_\ell$: if $1<\ell<N$, use $a_\ell=100,b_\ell=110$ on clock bits $(\ell-1,\ell,\ell+1)$; for $\ell=1$, use $a_1=00,b_1=10$ on bits $(1,2)$; for $\ell=N$, use $a_N=10,b_N=11$ on bits $(N-1,N)$. For a clock pattern $a$, let $|a\rangle\langle a|$ act on those listed clock bits and as identity on all other clock bits. Define the five-local propagation term
$$h_\ell=\frac12\left[I_{\rm data}\otimes(|a_\ell\rangle\langle a_\ell|+|b_\ell\rangle\langle b_\ell|)-U_\ell\otimes|b_\ell\rangle\langle a_\ell|-U_\ell^*\otimes|a_\ell\rangle\langle b_\ell|\right],\qquad H_{\rm prop}=\sum_{\ell=1}^Nh_\ell.$$

4. Put $K_0=n+3N$ and $\Delta_0=1/(216(N+1)^3)$, and choose the positive integer
$$J=2K_0+4K_0^2/\Delta_0+1.$$
Output the linearly interpolated Hamiltonian
$$H(s)=(1-s)H_{\rm init}+sH_{\rm final},\quad H_{\rm init}=H_{\rm input}+H_{\rm clock0}+JH_{\rm clock},\quad H_{\rm final}=H_{\rm input}+H_{\rm prop}+JH_{\rm clock}.$$
The term list, integer coefficient $J$, initial preparation, term-access queries, coefficient bits, gate costs, and generator time are explicit coordinates of the path access model ([[def-qa-36-adiabatic-resource-model]]); no spectral projector supplies $A_0$. With $M=n+3N-1$ terms, record the rational certificates $M_1=3N$ for the derivative and $B=M^2J^2$ for every sampled commutator sum; the coefficient functions are the exact constants $1,J$ and affine functions $s,1-s$.

5. Set $\Delta_0=1/[216(N+1)^3]$, $\gamma=3\Delta_0/4$, $B_T=6N/\gamma^2+63N^2/\gamma^3$, and $T=\lceil4B_T/\varepsilon\rceil$. Set the finite-precision simulation tolerance to $\varepsilon_{\rm sim}=\varepsilon/4$. These are finite rational computations.

6. Invoke [[alg-qa-36-discretized-path-simulation]] on the constructed path-access instance with evolution time $T$ and tolerance $\varepsilon_{\rm sim}$. Its output schedule applies the supplied $A_0$ before the path evolution, using each term's declared circuit-family or named-oracle provider. If any required term provider, coefficient evaluation or supported call is unavailable, return no schedule.

7. Declare the data register as the output and the clock register as discarded by the output procedure passed to step 6 (the resulting state is the partial trace over the clock, [[def-qc-partial-trace]]). Record $T$, preparation, simulation calls, coefficient precision, circuit-description and generator costs separately.

An **adiabatic path access instance** consists of a finite path model ([[def-qa-36-finite-adiabatic-path-model]]), its exact initial preparation circuit $A_0$ and cost $C_{\rm init}$, a finite term count $r$, and a uniform description
$$H(s)=\sum_{j=1}^r c_j(s)H_j,$$
where the $H_j$ are stated finite-dimensional self-adjoint operators and the real coefficient functions $c_j$ have explicit rational binary inputs, uniform evaluation procedures, certified value errors and certified first-derivative bound $M_1\ge\sup_s\|H'(s)\|$. Each inverse or controlled call is available only when separately declared. This is the finite term-list access interface of [[def-qa-20-simulation-error-and-cost-model]] and [[def-qa-20-term-list-access-model]].

The resource record lists separately: $C_{\rm init}$; the term count $r$; all term-oracle queries; controlled and inverse calls; gate, clean-ancilla and dirty-ancilla counts; coefficient-precision bits; full circuit-description bits; uniform generator time; and the continuous evolution time $T$. If a physical energy-normalized action is used, it also records $T\sup_s\|H(s)\|$. A missing coordinate is unavailable, not zero. $$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$
